recentItems.title: US President Trump arrives at Dublin airport to attend the 2026 Amgen Irish Open
recentItems.description:
(12 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Dublin - 12 September 2026
1. Various of US President Donald Trump arriving at Dublin airport, greeted by Tánaiste and Minister for Finance, Simon Harris; Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade, and Minister for Defence, Helen McEntee; Ambassador of Ireland to the United States of America, Ms. Geraldine Byrne Nason; Ambassador of The United States of America to Ireland, Mr. Edward Walsh; Mrs. Lynn Walsh, and Ms. Patricia O'Brien, Chief of Protocol
STORYLINE:
US President Donald Trump arrived at Dublin airport on Saturday to attend the 2026 Amgen Irish Open, which is being held at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg, County Clare.

Trump will hold talks with Ireland's president and prime minister, kicking off a weekend visit that's more about a major golf tournament held on a course he owns on the country's Atlantic coast.

The American president is set for separate meetings in Dublin with President of Ireland Catherine Connolly and Prime Minister Micheál Martin. Trump also plans remarks to U.S. and Irish business leaders at the U.S. ambassador's official residence in Dublin before traveling to his oceanfront golf club in Doonbeg, on the other side of the country, to watch the Irish Open.

The visit, the latest example of the blending of Trump's official duties with his personal interests, has gotten under the skin of some Dubliners.

Police put up a cordon around Dublin’s 1,750-acre (700-hectare) Phoenix Park, where he’ll meet Martin, the taoiseach, at the government’s Farmleigh state guesthouse, say hello to the president at her residence, Áras an Uachtaráin, and stop by Deerfield, the U.S. ambassador’s residence.

Separately, a collection of left-leaning opposition parties, anti-military groups, pro-Palestinian organizations, environmentalists and others plan to demonstrate against Trump in Dublin on Saturday.

Trump flew overnight to Ireland after observing the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, Washington and Pennsylvania. The Republican president spent the two nights before Friday's solemn observance giving lengthy speeches at a political pep rally in Dallas.

Martin invited Trump to visit Ireland when they met at the White House on St. Patrick's Day this year, and Ireland's political leaders will likely see the visit as a chance to maintain warm trans-Atlantic relations despite differences over trade and foreign policy, issues the White House said Trump wants to discuss.

Martin said before Trump arrived that he looked forward to discussing issues of “mutual interest” and "reaffirming the strong economic, cultural and people-to-people ties between Ireland and the United States.”

Martin also said he hopes to see an Irish winner lifting the trophy on Sunday. Ireland’s Shane Lowry topped the leader board at the tournament's halfway point.

Trump is an avid golfer who plays just about every weekend at clubs he owns in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events — and having a hand in organizing some of them in ways that benefit his family business. His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have each hosted professional golf tournaments this year.

The Irish Open is the second European Tour event to be held at a Trump property this year. The Nexo Championship was held last month at Trump's golf course in Aberdeen, Scotland.

recentItems.title: Families of prisoners still incarcerated in Brazil demand their immediate release
recentItems.description:
(12 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

++CHANGES WRONG TITLE FOR MARCO RUBIO FROM 'SENATOR' TO THE CORRECT TITLE 'U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE' IN SOUNDBITE IN SHOT 10 AND ANNOTATION++

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Caracas, Venezuela – 11 September 2026
1. Relatives of political prisoners marching with banners and photographs of detainees
2. Protesters gathered on steps holding letters spelling out (Spanish) “Free them all now”
3. Sign reading (Spanish) “Cilia (Flores, former first lady) asks for humanity; political prisoners were denied it”
4. Protesters holding photographs and letters
5. Man speaking through megaphone while holding Venezuelan flag
6. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Andreina Baduel, relative of prisoner:
"The acting president has a lot of answers to give the victims, because while she talks about reconciliation and peace, in the prisons political prisoners are being tortured and subjected to cruel treatment—and we will not allow that. Our demand is clear: the full and immediate release of all political prisoners. Today we are going to submit a document here in Miraflores, in which the first demand is the full release of all political prisoners." 
7. Protesters on steps holding handwritten signs, photographs and Venezuelan flag
8. Protesters standing with banners and cardboard signs
9. Handwritten cardboard signs, woman picking them up
10. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Vivian Mora Chang, 47, activist: 
"Mr. U.S. Secretary of State, Marco Rubio. Conduct a genuine investigation, make the findings public, and take action—so that no one else is shielded by political negotiations. Marco Rubio, listen to Venezuela—to its organized civil society, to those of us here—who are being identified by your own administration as ringleaders and held in your own federal prison. Avoid mistakes and do not grant house arrest or prison terms to the mastermind and perpetrator of crimes against humanity (she means Flores). And here’s just one example: all of us here—all the prisoners who have been held for more than 2,000 days, so-called terrorists convicted by the very judges they themselves appointed."
11. Various of women kneeling and rubbing a banner spread on the ground
STORYLINE:
Relatives of political prisoners marched near Venezuela’s presidential palace in Caracas on Friday, demanding their loved ones be released and criticising former first lady Cilia Flores’ request for house arrest in the United States.

Carrying photographs of detainees, protesters gathered on steps painted with the eyes of late President Hugo Chávez and held up letters spelling out “Free them all now.” One sign read: “Cilia asks for humanity; political prisoners were denied it.”

Flores’ lawyers asked a U.S. judge Wednesday to allow her to await trial on drug trafficking charges under home confinement, citing a heart condition they said had worsened in jail. They proposed round-the-clock armed surveillance and restrictions on visitors. Flores and her husband, former President Nicolás Maduro, have pleaded not guilty. 

Andreina Baduel said the families planned to submit a document at Miraflores Palace demanding the immediate and unconditional release of all political prisoners. She accused authorities of torturing detainees and subjecting them to cruel treatment, challenging the acting president’s calls for reconciliation and peace.

Protester Vivian Mora Chang urged U.S. officials to reject house arrest for Flores and investigate alleged crimes against humanity, saying political negotiations should not shield those responsible.

AP video by Brayan Antequero

recentItems.title: Dublin residents express mixed views ahead of Trump's visit to Ireland
recentItems.description:
(12 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTIONS SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Dublin, Ireland - 11 September 2026
1. Wide of Police on street
2. SOUNDBITE (English) Christopher Fox, taxi driver:
++OVERLAID BY SHOT 3,4,5++
"The majority of the people of Ireland don't want him (Trump) here. The man's causing trouble all over the world. There's no peace. And to think he has the power to push that button, people are in big trouble, you know. Sit down and talk with people. Don't be bombing them out of it."
3. US and Irish flags on building
4. Blocked road at entrance to Phoenix Park ahead of U.S. President Donald Trump's visit
5. Mid of road sign 
6. Police on street
7. SOUNDBITE (English) Donal Lunny, musician:
He's welcome here, welcome to play golf, etc. And maybe if it was left at that, that'd be fine."
++OVERLAID BY SHOT 8++
8. Wide of street, police 
9. SOUNDBITE (English) Diarmuid Coyle, student:
++OVERLAID BY SHOT 10, 11++
"And although, I suppose not everyone may be happy with Donald Trump's demeanour and policies, I think it's important that regardless the bond with our good friends the United States stays strong and in doing that we must cooperate with any visit they have."
10. Wide of bridge
11. Close of sign reading (English) 'Road Closed'
++ENDS ON SOUNDBITE++
STORYLINE:
People in Ireland expressed mixed views about U.S. President Donald Trump’s upcoming visit to the country.

Trump is flying to Ireland after observing the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the United States, which killed more than 3,000 people in New York, Washington and Pennsylvania.

The president plans to spend the weekend at his eponymous golf resort in Doonbeg on Ireland’s Atlantic coast, where the Irish Open is being held.

"The majority of the people of Ireland don't want him here," said Christopher Fox, a taxi driver from Dublin.

But student Diarmuid Coyle said the relationship between Ireland and the United States was more important than differences over one president.

Trump is scheduled to meet Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin on Saturday for talks on trade and international issues. He will also meet with Irish President Catherine Connolly and address business leaders at the U.S. ambassador’s residence.

Trump was invited to attend the Irish Open by Martin during the prime minister’s visit to Washington in March. He may also present the winner’s trophy on Sunday.

The U.S. and Ireland share strong historical and economic ties. About 30 million Americans claim Irish heritage, while more than 1 million Americans visit Ireland each year.

American technology and pharmaceutical companies also employ more than 200,000 people in Ireland and contribute billions of dollars in corporate tax.

Ireland is a member of the European Union, which has frequently drawn Trump’s criticism, but the country’s lucrative pharmaceutical sector has so far avoided steep U.S. tariffs.

AP video by Kwiyeon Ha

recentItems.title: Philippines coastguard brings bodies to shore after fire guts passenger ferry, killing at least 35
recentItems.description:
(12 Sep 2026) 
Clients note: This item contains on-screen graphics, including AP branding.

RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Port of Borac, Coron,  Philippines - 12 September 2026 
1. Emergency crew unloading bags containing remains of people killed in ferry fire disaster 
2. Various of emergency crew carrying body bags to makeshift tent ashore



STORYLINE:
A Philippine Coast Guard vessel arrived at Port of Borac on Saturday with bags containing the remains of people killed in a ferry fire disaster. 

The death toll rose to 35 people on Friday, after more bodies were recovered by emergency service personnel, from the burnt vessel near southwestern Palawan Province. 

Fifty-four people remain missing after the fire tore through the ferry Wednesday night.

There were 43 survivors. 

The ferry sailed from the capital, Manila, and was around 7.4 kilometers (4.5 miles) off the village of Turda near its destination of Coron in Palawan province when the fire was reported. 

The cause of the fire has not been determined.

According to the manifest, 134 people were onboard, 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. 

The 53-meter (174-foot) vessel had a capacity to carry 306 passengers and 27 crew. 

Coron is a popular tourist destination known for clear blue waters, limestone cliffs and rock formations.

Ferries are frequently used for transport in the Philippine archipelago. 

Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces.

In 1987, the ferry Dona Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker in the central Philippines, killing more than 4,300 people in the world’s deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.

recentItems.title: Philippines coastguard on retrieval of bodies and ongoing investigation after ferry fire disaster
recentItems.description:
(12 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Manila, Philippines - 12 September 2026 
1. Sign of MV June Aster ferry incident at Philippine Coast Guard headquarters
2. Members of Philippine Coast Guard and media arrive for press conference
3. Wide of press conference
4. SOUNDBITE (English, Tagalog), Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, Philippine Coast Guard Spokesperson: 
“Currently we are focused on the retrieval and after that we will proceed with the investigation. For the safety investigation, we have already started the conduct of inquiry from the survivors onboard the vessel.”
5. Wide of press conference
6. SOUNDBITE (English, Tagalog), Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, Philippine Coast Guard Spokesperson: 
“Based on the statement of the witness, everything happened so fast. We will review everything. I always mention that there may be a probability of a liability from the crew, from the captain and the shipping company.”
7. Cutaway of cameramen during press conference
8. SOUNDBITE (English, Tagalog), Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, Philippine Coast Guard Spokesperson: 
"The captain of the ship remains at large. Because all of the survivors that time were on the list. But as we speak, the name of the captain is not on the list. Although I heard some information that the captain is still alive. But as we speak, we have no statement or any communication as to the status of the captain of the vessel.” 
9. Cutaway of reporters during press conference
10. SOUNDBITE (English, Tagalog), Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, Philippine Coast Guard Spokesperson: 
“With the numbers of missing, with the numbers of causality, definitely the captain has a big responsibility. So, as I said, the captain of the ship is the ship’s captain; all its cargo, passengers, from its port of origin to its port of destination, is responsible for transporting them safely. As to the incident, with the numbers of casualty, definitely the captain has a responsibility and liability."
11. Commodore Geronimo Bautista Tuvilla, Philippine Coast Guard speaking to news reporter 
12. SOUNDBITE (English, Tagalog), Commodore Geronimo Bautista Tuvilla, Philippine Coast Guard, incident management for MV June Aster: 
“We cannot speculate. But of course, it’s a joint investigation. We have tapped the experts also of the PNP (Philippine National Police). Our commandant also requested their presence there. It’s a composite team right now. We will gather everything from technical experts and all to determine the root cause.” 
13. Wide of Tuvilla speaking 
14. SOUNDBITE (English, Tagalog), Commodore Geronimo Bautista Tuvilla, Philippine Coast Guard, incident management for MV June Aster: 
“This is not a first time incident involving a fire. We will look at everything. Are there also cases similar to it abroad about what we are speculating about. We cannot just rule out anything. We will determine that. Everything will be determined.”
15. Wide of press conference
STORYLINE:
Members of the Philippine Coast Guard delivered an update on Saturday into the fire that gutted a passenger ferry, killing at least 35 people.

Fifty-four people are still missing since the fire tore through the ferry Wednesday night near southwestern Palawan province. There were 43 survivors. 

Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said efffort were still focussed on the retrieval of bodies from the ferry. 

The cause of the fire has not been determined.

She said the captain remained at large. 


Coron is a popular tourist destination known for clear blue waters, limestone cliffs and rock formations.

recentItems.title: Philippines coastguard brings bodies to shore after fire guts passenger ferry, killing at least 35
recentItems.description:
(12 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Port of Borac, Coron, Palawan, Philippines - 12 September 2026 
1. Zoom in to Philippine Coast Guard vessel arriving at Port of Borac with emergency crew on board, including several wearing hazmat suits, with bags containing the remains of people killed in ferry fire disaster
2. Mid of emergency crew standing on vessel next to bags containing remains of victims
3. Pan of Philippine Coast Guard vessel 
4. Crew unloading items 
5. Mid of personnel on vessel as it docks
6. Mid of smaller boat with personnel on board
7. Wide of Philippine Coast Guard vessel 
8. Pan of personnel on docked vessel
9. Zoom out of personnel on docked vessel
STORYLINE:
A Philippine Coast Guard vessel arrived at Port of Boracon Saturday with an emergency crew on board, including several members wearing hazmat suits, 

AP video also showed bags containing the remains of people killed in ferry fire disaster

The death toll from the Philippines ferry fire disaster rose to 35 people on Friday, after more bodies were recovered by emergency service personnel, from the burnt vessel near southwestern Palawan Province. 

Fifty-four people remain missing after the fire tore through the ferry Wednesday night.

There were 43 survivors. 

Rescuers on Thursday struggled to get inside the vessel because of the heat and smoke, slowing efforts to search for passengers who may have been trapped. 

On Friday, the death toll rose to 35 as more bodies were recovered.

Emergency personnel, some wearing hazmat suits, were seen standing aboard a Philippine Coast Guard vessel as it docked at Port of Borac in Coron, with the remains of those killed in the ferry fire in bags on board. 

The ferry sailed from the capital, Manila, and was around 7.4 kilometers (4.5 miles) off the village of Turda near its destination of Coron in Palawan province when the fire was reported. 

The cause of the fire has not been determined.

According to the manifest, 134 people were onboard, 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. 

The 53-meter (174-foot) vessel had a capacity to carry 306 passengers and 27 crew. 

Two passengers listed in the manifest reported to authorities that they failed to board, the coast guard said. 

Two of the survivors were tourists from Chile, according to Rachel Conserman, a staffer of the ship’s owner Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc. 

They were recovering from injuries in a hospital in Coron, she said, adding that no other foreigners were known to have been on the ship.

Coron is a popular tourist destination known for clear blue waters, limestone cliffs and rock formations.

Ferries are frequently used for transport in the Philippine archipelago. 

Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces.

In 1987, the ferry Dona Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker in the central Philippines, killing more than 4,300 people in the world’s deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.

recentItems.title: After tragedy, a Greek couple welcomes a daughter born from an embryo frozen for 22 years
recentItems.description:
(12 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTIONS SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Athens, Greece -  11 September 2026
1. Close-up of newborn baby girl
2. Wide of maternity ward room with couple looking at baby
3. Close-up of Constantinos Raptis, left, and Cristina Rapti-Tzelepi looking at baby
4. Medium of couple
5. Close-up of balloon reading (English) "It’s a girl"
6. Various of fertility clinic
7. Close-up of monitor displaying embryos belonging to Rapti-Tzelepi and Raptis
8. SOUNDBITE (Greek) Cristina Rapti-Tzelepi, mother:++PARTLY OVERLAID BY SHOTS 1-7++
"After 22 years, an accident occurred and we lost our child. Sometime later—even while in deep mourning—we decided to make use of the embryos that were already cryopreserved. Due to time constraints and the strict age limits imposed by the legal framework, we had to act very quickly."
9. Various of fertility clinic
10. Staff member lifting frozen sperm samples from container
11. SOUNDBITE (English) Dr. Kostas Pantos, gynecologist and IVF specialist: ++PARTLY OVERLAID BY SHOTS 9-10, 12++
"It’s  the first time that after 22 and a half years an embryo of the couple, autologous embryo, their own embryo, has been thawed and implanted and delivered as a live birth."
12. Raptis walking with baby
13. Close-up of baby’s feet 
14. Wide of couple and baby
15. Close-up of baby sleeping on father’s shoulder
16. SOUNDBITE (Greek) Constantinos Raptis, father: ++PARTLY OVERLAID BY SHOTS 12-15, 17-18++
"Along with the little one came the oxygen that enabled us to breathe and get on with our lives because we were living in absolute darkness. For us, the world had been lost. Mr. Pantos was our companion on this journey. He took us by the hand and pulled us out of our deepest darkness."
17. Mid of baby with parents standing over her
18. Close-up of baby
STORYLINE:
Out of their darkest moment, a Greek couple managed to make a new start with a baby born this week. Doing so meant using one of her decades-old embryos and racing to beat a government deadline.

Just months after their 21 year old son died in a road crash in October, Cristina Rapti Tzelepi, now 54, and her husband made the decision to pursue another attempt using an embryo frozen for 22 years.

Rapti-Tzelepi was running up against the Greek government's 54-year age limit for women to complete in vitro fertilization procedures and secure approval from a national authority. When she started, time was already running short.

She gave birth to a girl on Wednesday in Greek capital Athens who weighed in at 3.49 kilograms (7 pounds, 11 ounces). In a hospital room brightened with pink balloons and flowers on Friday, the new parents were overcome with emotion.

The child was born using the woman’s embryo that had been frozen more than 22 years ago, an unusually long time for a frozen fertilized egg to be used to produce a pregnancy.

Last year, an Ohio couple welcomed a baby boy developed from an embryo frozen for more than 30 years through a process known as “embryo adoption,” and earned recognition from Guinness World Records.

Dr. Kostas Pantos, Rapti-Tzelepi's gynecologist and head of the Hellenic Society of Reproductive Medicine, argued that Greece’s age restrictions warrant review, noting the country’s steep birth rate decline.

The baby’s 60-year-old father, Constantinos Raptis, held his new daughter as she slept on his shoulder, wrapped in a white bodysuit. He said that he's deeply grateful to the doctor for restoring hope to his family.


AP Video by Lefteris Pitarakis. Production by Theodora Tongas
